title: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Rudimentary, atrophied or aborted organs that bear the stamp of uselessness are extremely common in animals and plants.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Organs or parts in this strange condition, bearing the stamp of inutility, are extremely common throughout nature.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained”. Scope: animals and plants generally

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-22: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Prevalence is in principle straightforward, but rudimentary status requires interpretation. Existing databases contain many examples without representative sampling across nature.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define rudimentary organs by reduced size or function relative to homologues and estimate their prevalence across a stratified sample of animal and plant taxa. A high prevalence across major clades supports 'extremely common'; consistently low prevalence refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Databases do not systematically record vestigial organs or true absences.

Uselessness is often unknown and reduction thresholds are subjective.

Published morphology overrepresents unusual structures.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.48
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A taxonomic census with a pre-registered threshold would decide the frequency claim, but that census has not been assembled as a dataset. Narrative lists in the anatomical literature are too uneven to estimate a rate, and gene-loss catalogues would answer a different question about pseudogenes. The analysis cannot be run until the variables are collected and coded.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using an explicit definition of a rudimentary organ as a reduced homolog with little or no current function, estimate the fraction of species or higher taxa that bear at least one, with a pre-set threshold for 'extremely common'. The claim is confirmed if that fraction exceeds the threshold across animals and plants, and refuted if rudiments are confined to a small minority of taxa.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Functionlessness is disputed for many classic rudiments, so the objects to be counted are unstable.

'Extremely common' has no numerical boundary, which must be set before any count can decide the claim.

No public dataset inventories rudimentary organs across animals and plants.
